# PATTERN 1: EVENT FILTERING PATTERN
# Purpose: Filter events based on specific criteria/conditions
# ============================================================================

def event_filtering_pattern():
    """
    Event Filtering Pattern: Select only events that meet specific criteria.
    Use cases: Anomaly detection, threshold monitoring, specific event selection
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("PATTERN 1: EVENT FILTERING PATTERN")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Sample event data
    event_data = [
        ("evt001", "login", "user123", "2024-01-15 10:00:00", 1, "success"),
        ("evt002", "purchase", "user456", "2024-01-15 10:05:00", 150, "success"),
        ("evt003", "login", "user789", "2024-01-15 10:10:00", 3, "failed"),
        ("evt004", "purchase", "user123", "2024-01-15 10:15:00", 500, "success"),
        ("evt005", "login", "user456", "2024-01-15 10:20:00", 1, "success"),
        ("evt006", "purchase", "user789", "2024-01-15 10:25:00", 75, "success"),
        ("evt007", "login", "user999", "2024-01-15 10:30:00", 5, "failed"),
        ("evt008", "purchase", "user123", "2024-01-15 10:35:00", 1200, "success"),
    ]
    
    schema = StructType([
        StructField("event_id", StringType(), True),
        StructField("event_type", StringType(), True),
        StructField("user_id", StringType(), True),
        StructField("timestamp", StringType(), True),
        StructField("value", IntegerType(), True),
        StructField("status", StringType(), True)
    ])
    
    events_df = spark.createDataFrame(event_data, schema) \
        .withColumn("timestamp", col("timestamp").cast(TimestampType()))
    
    print("\nOriginal Events:")
    events_df.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Filter 1: High-value transactions (value > 100)
    high_value_events = events_df.filter(
        (col("event_type") == "purchase") & (col("value") > 100)
    )
    
    print("\nFiltered: High-Value Purchases (> 100):")
    high_value_events.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Filter 2: Failed login attempts
    failed_logins = events_df.filter(
        (col("event_type") == "login") & (col("status") == "failed")
    )
    
    print("\nFiltered: Failed Login Attempts:")
    failed_logins.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Filter 3: Complex filtering - Multiple attempts or high value
    suspicious_events = events_df.filter(
        ((col("event_type") == "login") & (col("value") > 2)) |
        ((col("event_type") == "purchase") & (col("value") > 1000))
    )
    
    print("\nFiltered: Suspicious Events (Multiple login attempts or very high purchases):")
    suspicious_events.show(truncate=False)
    
    return events_df


# ============================================================================
# PATTERN 2: EVENT TRANSFORMATION PATTERN
# Purpose: Transform event data into different formats or enrich with additional info
# ============================================================================

def event_transformation_pattern(events_df):
    """
    Event Transformation Pattern: Convert events from one format to another.
    Use cases: Data enrichment, format conversion, field derivation
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("PATTERN 2: EVENT TRANSFORMATION PATTERN")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Transformation 1: Enrich events with derived fields
    transformed_events = events_df \
        .withColumn("event_category", 
            when(col("event_type") == "login", "authentication")
            .when(col("event_type") == "purchase", "transaction")
            .otherwise("other")
        ) \
        .withColumn("risk_level",
            when((col("event_type") == "login") & (col("value") > 2), "high")
            .when((col("event_type") == "purchase") & (col("value") > 500), "high")
            .when(col("status") == "failed", "medium")
            .otherwise("low")
        ) \
        .withColumn("hour_of_day", expr("hour(timestamp)")) \
        .withColumn("is_business_hours", 
            when((col("hour_of_day") >= 9) & (col("hour_of_day") <= 17), True)
            .otherwise(False)
        )
    
    print("\nTransformed Events with Derived Fields:")
    transformed_events.select(
        "event_id", "event_type", "event_category", "risk_level", 
        "hour_of_day", "is_business_hours", "value"
    ).show(truncate=False)
    
    # Transformation 2: Normalize and standardize
    normalized_events = transformed_events \
        .withColumn("normalized_value", 
            expr("value / 1000.0")  # Normalize to thousands
        ) \
        .withColumn("event_type_upper", expr("upper(event_type)")) \
        .withColumn("user_id_hash", expr("md5(user_id)"))
    
    print("\nNormalized Events:")
    normalized_events.select(
        "event_id", "event_type_upper", "normalized_value", "user_id_hash"
    ).show(truncate=False)
    
    # Transformation 3: Complex transformation with UDF-like logic
    complex_transformed = transformed_events \
        .withColumn("event_score",
            when(col("risk_level") == "high", col("value") * 3)
            .when(col("risk_level") == "medium", col("value") * 2)
            .otherwise(col("value"))
        ) \
        .withColumn("event_metadata", 
            struct(
                col("event_category"),
                col("risk_level"),
                col("is_business_hours")
            )
        )
    
    print("\nComplex Transformed Events with Scoring:")
    complex_transformed.select(
        "event_id", "event_type", "value", "event_score", "event_metadata"
    ).show(truncate=False)
    
    return transformed_events


# ============================================================================
# PATTERN 3: EVENT AGGREGATION PATTERN
# Purpose: Aggregate events over time windows or by dimensions
# ============================================================================

def event_aggregation_pattern(events_df):
    """
    Event Aggregation Pattern: Summarize events using various aggregation functions.
    Use cases: Real-time analytics, KPI calculation, trend analysis
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("PATTERN 3: EVENT AGGREGATION PATTERN")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Aggregation 1: Group by event type
    type_aggregation = events_df.groupBy("event_type") \
        .agg(
            count("*").alias("event_count"),
            _sum("value").alias("total_value"),
            avg("value").alias("avg_value"),
            _max("value").alias("max_value"),
            _min("value").alias("min_value")
        )
    
    print("\nAggregation by Event Type:")
    type_aggregation.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Aggregation 2: Group by user
    user_aggregation = events_df.groupBy("user_id") \
        .agg(
            count("*").alias("total_events"),
            count(when(col("event_type") == "login", 1)).alias("login_count"),
            count(when(col("event_type") == "purchase", 1)).alias("purchase_count"),
            _sum("value").alias("total_spent"),
            collect_list("event_type").alias("event_types")
        ) \
        .orderBy(col("total_spent").desc())
    
    print("\nAggregation by User:")
    user_aggregation.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Aggregation 3: Time-based windowed aggregation (5-minute windows)
    # First, we need to create more granular timestamps for demonstration
    windowed_aggregation = events_df \
        .withColumn("timestamp", col("timestamp").cast(TimestampType())) \
        .groupBy(
            window(col("timestamp"), "10 minutes"),
            col("event_type")
        ) \
        .agg(
            count("*").alias("events_in_window"),
            _sum("value").alias("total_value"),
            avg("value").alias("avg_value")
        ) \
        .orderBy("window")
    
    print("\nTime-Windowed Aggregation (10-minute windows):")
    windowed_aggregation.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Aggregation 4: Multi-dimensional aggregation with rollup
    multi_dim_aggregation = events_df.rollup("event_type", "status") \
        .agg(
            count("*").alias("count"),
            _sum("value").alias("total_value")
        ) \
        .orderBy("event_type", "status")
    
    print("\nMulti-dimensional Aggregation with Rollup:")
    multi_dim_aggregation.show(truncate=False)
    
    return user_aggregation


# ============================================================================
# PATTERN 4: EVENT CORRELATION PATTERN
# Purpose: Correlate related events to identify patterns and relationships
# ============================================================================

def event_correlation_pattern():
    """
    Event Correlation Pattern: Find relationships between different events.
    Use cases: User journey analysis, fraud detection, behavior patterns
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("PATTERN 4: EVENT CORRELATION PATTERN")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Create correlated event data
    correlated_data = [
        ("evt001", "user123", "page_view", "2024-01-15 10:00:00", "homepage"),
        ("evt002", "user123", "add_to_cart", "2024-01-15 10:02:00", "product_A"),
        ("evt003", "user123", "purchase", "2024-01-15 10:05:00", "product_A"),
        ("evt004", "user456", "page_view", "2024-01-15 10:01:00", "homepage"),
        ("evt005", "user456", "add_to_cart", "2024-01-15 10:03:00", "product_B"),
        ("evt006", "user456", "cart_abandon", "2024-01-15 10:10:00", "product_B"),
        ("evt007", "user789", "login", "2024-01-15 10:00:00", None),
        ("evt008", "user789", "failed_payment", "2024-01-15 10:05:00", "product_C"),
        ("evt009", "user789", "purchase", "2024-01-15 10:07:00", "product_C"),
    ]
    
    schema = StructType([
        StructField("event_id", StringType(), True),
        StructField("user_id", StringType(), True),
        StructField("event_type", StringType(), True),
        StructField("timestamp", StringType(), True),
        StructField("product", StringType(), True)
    ])
    
    events_df = spark.createDataFrame(correlated_data, schema) \
        .withColumn("timestamp", col("timestamp").cast(TimestampType()))
    
    print("\nOriginal Correlated Events:")
    events_df.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Correlation 1: Find event sequences per user
    window_spec = Window.partitionBy("user_id").orderBy("timestamp")
    
    sequenced_events = events_df \
        .withColumn("prev_event", lag("event_type", 1).over(window_spec)) \
        .withColumn("next_event", lead("event_type", 1).over(window_spec)) \
        .withColumn("event_sequence_num", row_number().over(window_spec))
    
    print("\nEvent Sequences with Previous and Next Events:")
    sequenced_events.select(
        "user_id", "event_sequence_num", "prev_event", 
        "event_type", "next_event", "timestamp"
    ).show(truncate=False)
    
    # Correlation 2: Identify conversion funnels
    conversion_funnel = events_df \
        .groupBy("user_id") \
        .agg(
            collect_list(struct("timestamp", "event_type", "product")).alias("events")
        ) \
        .withColumn("has_page_view", 
            expr("exists(events, x -> x.event_type = 'page_view')")
        ) \
        .withColumn("has_add_to_cart", 
            expr("exists(events, x -> x.event_type = 'add_to_cart')")
        ) \
        .withColumn("has_purchase", 
            expr("exists(events, x -> x.event_type = 'purchase')")
        ) \
        .withColumn("conversion_stage",
            when(col("has_purchase"), "converted")
            .when(col("has_add_to_cart"), "cart_added")
            .when(col("has_page_view"), "viewed")
            .otherwise("unknown")
        )
    
    print("\nConversion Funnel Analysis:")
    conversion_funnel.select(
        "user_id", "has_page_view", "has_add_to_cart", 
        "has_purchase", "conversion_stage"
    ).show(truncate=False)
    
    # Correlation 3: Time-based correlation - events within time window
    self_joined = events_df.alias("e1").join(
        events_df.alias("e2"),
        (col("e1.user_id") == col("e2.user_id")) &
        (col("e1.event_id") != col("e2.event_id")) &
        (col("e2.timestamp") > col("e1.timestamp")) &
        (unix_timestamp(col("e2.timestamp")) - unix
```python
_timestamp(col("e1.timestamp")) <= 300)  # Within 5 minutes
    )
    
    correlated_pairs = self_joined.select(
        col("e1.user_id"),
        col("e1.event_type").alias("first_event"),
        col("e1.timestamp").alias("first_timestamp"),
        col("e2.event_type").alias("second_event"),
        col("e2.timestamp").alias("second_timestamp"),
        ((unix_timestamp(col("e2.timestamp")) - 
          unix_timestamp(col("e1.timestamp"))) / 60).alias("time_diff_minutes")
    ).orderBy("user_id", "first_timestamp")
    
    print("\nCorrelated Event Pairs (within 5 minutes):")
    correlated_pairs.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Correlation 4: Pattern detection - specific event sequences
    pattern_detection = sequenced_events \
        .filter(
            (col("prev_event") == "add_to_cart") & 
            (col("event_type") == "cart_abandon")
        )
    
    print("\nDetected Pattern: Add to Cart -> Cart Abandon:")
    pattern_detection.select(
        "user_id", "prev_event", "event_type", "product", "timestamp"
    ).show(truncate=False)
    
    return events_df


# ============================================================================
# PATTERN 5: EVENT SEQUENCING PATTERN
# Purpose: Order and sequence events to understand temporal relationships
# ============================================================================

def event_sequencing_pattern():
    """
    Event Sequencing Pattern: Order events and analyze sequences.
    Use cases: Process flow analysis, state machine tracking, workflow monitoring
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("PATTERN 5: EVENT SEQUENCING PATTERN")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Create sequence data
    sequence_data = [
        ("order001", "user123", "order_created", "2024-01-15 10:00:00", 1),
        ("order001", "user123", "payment_initiated", "2024-01-15 10:02:00", 2),
        ("order001", "user123", "payment_completed", "2024-01-15 10:03:00", 3),
        ("order001", "user123", "order_confirmed", "2024-01-15 10:04:00", 4),
        ("order001", "user123", "shipped", "2024-01-15 12:00:00", 5),
        ("order002", "user456", "order_created", "2024-01-15 10:05:00", 1),
        ("order002", "user456", "payment_initiated", "2024-01-15 10:06:00", 2),
        ("order002", "user456", "payment_failed", "2024-01-15 10:07:00", 3),
        ("order003", "user789", "order_created", "2024-01-15 10:10:00", 1),
        ("order003", "user789", "payment_initiated", "2024-01-15 10:11:00", 2),
        ("order003", "user789", "payment_completed", "2024-01-15 10:12:00", 3),
        ("order003", "user789", "order_confirmed", "2024-01-15 10:13:00", 4),
    ]
    
    schema = StructType([
        StructField("order_id", StringType(), True),
        StructField("user_id", StringType(), True),
        StructField("event_type", StringType(), True),
        StructField("timestamp", StringType(), True),
        StructField("sequence_num", IntegerType(), True)
    ])
    
    events_df = spark.createDataFrame(sequence_data, schema) \
        .withColumn("timestamp", col("timestamp").cast(TimestampType()))
    
    print("\nOriginal Event Sequences:")
    events_df.orderBy("order_id", "sequence_num").show(truncate=False)
    
    # Sequencing 1: Calculate time between sequential events
    window_spec = Window.partitionBy("order_id").orderBy("sequence_num")
    
    sequenced_with_timing = events_df \
        .withColumn("prev_timestamp", lag("timestamp", 1).over(window_spec)) \
        .withColumn("prev_event", lag("event_type", 1).over(window_spec)) \
        .withColumn("time_since_prev_event",
            when(col("prev_timestamp").isNotNull(),
                (unix_timestamp(col("timestamp")) - 
                 unix_timestamp(col("prev_timestamp"))) / 60
            ).otherwise(0)
        )
    
    print("\nSequenced Events with Timing:")
    sequenced_with_timing.select(
        "order_id", "sequence_num", "prev_event", "event_type", 
        "time_since_prev_event"
    ).orderBy("order_id", "sequence_num").show(truncate=False)
    
    # Sequencing 2: Build complete event sequences per order
    complete_sequences = events_df \
        .groupBy("order_id", "user_id") \
        .agg(
            collect_list(struct("sequence_num", "event_type", "timestamp")).alias("events"),
            count("*").alias("total_events"),
            _max("sequence_num").alias("max_sequence")
        ) \
        .withColumn("sorted_events", 
            expr("transform(array_sort(events, (left, right) -> " +
                 "case when left.sequence_num < right.sequence_num then -1 " +
                 "when left.sequence_num > right.sequence_num then 1 else 0 end), " +
                 "x -> x.event_type)")
        )
    
    print("\nComplete Event Sequences per Order:")
    complete_sequences.select(
        "order_id", "user_id", "total_events", "sorted_events"
    ).show(truncate=False)
    
    # Sequencing 3: Identify sequence completion status
    sequence_status = complete_sequences \
        .withColumn("is_complete",
            expr("array_contains(sorted_events, 'shipped')")
        ) \
        .withColumn("has_payment_failure",
            expr("array_contains(sorted_events, 'payment_failed')")
        ) \
        .withColumn("status",
            when(col("has_payment_failure"), "failed")
            .when(col("is_complete"), "completed")
            .otherwise("in_progress")
        )
    
    print("\nSequence Completion Status:")
    sequence_status.select(
        "order_id", "status", "total_events", "is_complete", "has_payment_failure"
    ).show(truncate=False)
    
    # Sequencing 4: Detect sequence anomalies (missing steps)
    expected_sequence = ["order_created", "payment_initiated", 
                        "payment_completed", "order_confirmed", "shipped"]
    
    sequence_validation = complete_sequences \
        .withColumn("missing_steps",
            expr(f"""
                filter(array({','.join([f"'{s}'" for s in expected_sequence])}),
                       x -> not array_contains(sorted_events, x))
            """)
        ) \
        .withColumn("has_anomaly", expr("size(missing_steps) > 0"))
    
    print("\nSequence Validation (Missing Steps):")
    sequence_validation.select(
        "order_id", "sorted_events", "missing_steps", "has_anomaly"
    ).show(truncate=False)
    
    return events_df


# ============================================================================
# PATTERN 6: OUT-OF-ORDER EVENT PATTERN
# Purpose: Handle events that arrive out of chronological order
# ============================================================================

def out_of_order_event_pattern():
    """
    Out-of-Order Event Pattern: Process events that arrive late or out of sequence.
    Use cases: Distributed systems, network delays, late-arriving data
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("PATTERN 6: OUT-OF-ORDER EVENT PATTERN")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Create out-of-order event data
    # Note: arrival_time != event_time (simulating late arrivals)
    ooo_data = [
        ("evt001", "sensor1", "2024-01-15 10:00:00", "2024-01-15 10:00:05", 100),
        ("evt002", "sensor1", "2024-01-15 10:01:00", "2024-01-15 10:01:02", 105),
        ("evt003", "sensor1", "2024-01-15 10:02:00", "2024-01-15 10:05:00", 110),  # Late arrival
        ("evt004", "sensor1", "2024-01-15 10:03:00", "2024-01-15 10:03:01", 115),
        ("evt005", "sensor1", "2024-01-15 10:04:00", "2024-01-15 10:04:03", 120),
        ("evt006", "sensor2", "2024-01-15 10:00:00", "2024-01-15 10:00:10", 200),
        ("evt007", "sensor2", "2024-01-15 10:01:00", "2024-01-15 10:10:00", 205),  # Very late
        ("evt008", "sensor2", "2024-01-15 10:02:00", "2024-01-15 10:02:05", 210),
        ("evt009", "sensor1", "2024-01-15 10:00:30", "2024-01-15 10:06:00", 102),  # Out of order
    ]
    
    schema = StructType([
        StructField("event_id", StringType(), True),
        StructField("sensor_id", StringType(), True),
        StructField("event_time", StringType(), True),
        StructField("arrival_time", StringType(), True),
        StructField("value", IntegerType(), True)
    ])
    
    events_df = spark.createDataFrame(ooo_data, schema) \
        .withColumn("event_time", col("event_time").cast(TimestampType())) \
        .withColumn("arrival_time", col("arrival_time").cast(TimestampType()))
    
    print("\nOut-of-Order Events (sorted by arrival time):")
    events_df.orderBy("arrival_time").show(truncate=False)
    
    # Pattern 1: Calculate lateness
    events_with_lateness = events_df \
        .withColumn("lateness_seconds",
            unix_timestamp(col("arrival_time")) - unix_timestamp(col("event_time"))
        ) \
        .withColumn("is_late", col("lateness_seconds") > 60) \
        .withColumn("lateness_category",
            when(col("lateness_seconds") <= 5, "on_time")
            .when(col("lateness_seconds") <= 60, "slightly_late")
            .when(col("lateness_seconds") <= 300, "late")
            .otherwise("very_late")
        )
    
    print("\nEvents with Lateness Analysis:")
    events_with_lateness.select(
        "event_id", "sensor_id", "event_time", "arrival_time", 
        "lateness_seconds", "lateness_category"
    ).orderBy("arrival_time").show(truncate=False)
    
    # Pattern 2: Reorder events by event_time (not arrival_time)
    properly_ordered = events_df.orderBy("sensor_id", "event_time")
    
    print("\nProperly Ordered Events (by event_time):")
    properly_ordered.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Pattern 3: Watermarking - identify events outside acceptable window
    window_spec = Window.partitionBy("sensor_id").orderBy("arrival_time")
    
    watermarked_events = events_with_lateness \
        .withColumn("max_event_time_so_far", 
            _max("event_time").over(
                window_spec.rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow)
            )
        ) \
        .withColumn("is_out_of_order",
            col("event_time") < col("max_event_time_so_far")
        ) \
        .withColumn("watermark_violation",
            when(col("is_out_of_order") & (col("lateness_seconds") > 120), True)
            .otherwise(False)
        )
    
    print("\nWatermarked Events (identifying out-of-order and violations):")
    watermarked_events.select(
        "event_id", "sensor_id", "event_time", "is_out_of_order", 
        "watermark_violation", "lateness_seconds"
    ).orderBy("sensor_id", "arrival_time").show(truncate=False)
    
    # Pattern 4: Buffering and reordering within time windows
    # Create sequence numbers based on both arrival and event time
    arrival_window = Window.partitionBy("sensor_id").orderBy("arrival_time")
    event_window = Window.partitionBy("sensor_id").orderBy("event_time")
    
    reordered_events = events_df \
        .withColumn("arrival_sequence", row_number().over(arrival_window)) \
        .withColumn("event_sequence", row_number().over(event_window)) \
        .withColumn("sequence_diff", 
            col("arrival_sequence") - col("event_sequence")
        ) \
        .withColumn("reordering_needed", col("sequence_diff") != 0)
    
    print("\nReordering Analysis:")
    reordered_events.select(
        "event_id", "sensor_id", "arrival_sequence", "event_sequence", 
        "sequence_diff", "reordering_needed"
    ).orderBy("sensor_id", "arrival_sequence").show(truncate=False)
    
    # Pattern 5: Aggregation with late data handling
    # Aggregate by 1-minute event_time windows
    windowed_aggregation = events_df \
        .groupBy(
            col("sensor_id"),
            window(col("event_time"), "1 minute")
        ) \
        .agg(
            count("*").alias("event_count"),
            avg("value").alias("avg_value"),
            _max("arrival_time").alias("last_arrival"),
            _max(unix_timestamp(col("arrival_time")) - 
                unix_timestamp(col("event_time"))).alias("max_lateness")
        ) \
        .orderBy("sensor_id", "window")
    
    print("\nWindowed Aggregation (handling out-of-order events):")
    windowed_aggregation.show(truncate=False)
    
    return events_df


# ============================================================================
# PATTERN 7: EVENT REPLAY PATTERN
# Purpose: Replay historical events for testing, debugging, or reprocessing
# ============================================================================

def event_replay_pattern():
    """
    Event Replay Pattern: Replay historical events in controlled manner.
    Use cases: Testing, debugging, data recovery, what-if analysis
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("PATTERN 7: EVENT REPLAY PATTERN")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Create historical event data
    historical_data = [
        ("evt001", "user123", "login", "2024-01-15 10:00:00", "v1", "success"),
        ("evt002", "
```python
user123", "purchase", "2024-01-15 10:05:00", "v1", "success"),
        ("evt003", "user456", "login", "2024-01-15 10:10:00", "v1", "success"),
        ("evt004", "user456", "purchase", "2024-01-15 10:15:00", "v1", "failed"),
        ("evt005", "user789", "login", "2024-01-15 10:20:00", "v1", "success"),
        ("evt006", "user789", "purchase", "2024-01-15 10:25:00", "v1", "success"),
        ("evt007", "user123", "refund", "2024-01-15 10:30:00", "v1", "success"),
        ("evt008", "user456", "purchase", "2024-01-15 10:35:00", "v1", "success"),
    ]
    
    schema = StructType([
        StructField("event_id", StringType(), True),
        StructField("user_id", StringType(), True),
        StructField("event_type", StringType(), True),
        StructField("original_timestamp", StringType(), True),
        StructField("version", StringType(), True),
        StructField("status", StringType(), True)
    ])
    
    events_df = spark.createDataFrame(historical_data, schema) \
        .withColumn("original_timestamp", col("original_timestamp").cast(TimestampType()))
    
    print("\nOriginal Historical Events:")
    events_df.orderBy("original_timestamp").show(truncate=False)
    
    # Replay Pattern 1: Full replay with new timestamps
    full_replay = events_df \
        .withColumn("replay_timestamp", current_timestamp()) \
        .withColumn("replay_id", monotonically_increasing_id()) \
        .withColumn("replay_version", lit("v2")) \
        .withColumn("is_replay", lit(True)) \
        .withColumn("replay_reason", lit("full_system_test"))
    
    print("\nFull Replay (all events with new timestamps):")
    full_replay.select(
        "event_id", "user_id", "event_type", "original_timestamp", 
        "replay_timestamp", "is_replay", "replay_version"
    ).show(truncate=False)
    
    # Replay Pattern 2: Selective replay (only failed events)
    selective_replay = events_df \
        .filter(col("status") == "failed") \
        .withColumn("replay_timestamp", current_timestamp()) \
        .withColumn("replay_attempt", lit(1)) \
        .withColumn("replay_reason", lit("retry_failed_events")) \
        .withColumn("original_status", col("status")) \
        .withColumn("status", lit("pending"))  # Reset status for retry
    
    print("\nSelective Replay (failed events only):")
    selective_replay.select(
        "event_id", "user_id", "event_type", "original_status", 
        "status", "replay_reason"
    ).show(truncate=False)
    
    # Replay Pattern 3: Time-range replay
    time_range_start = "2024-01-15 10:10:00"
    time_range_end = "2024-01-15 10:25:00"
    
    time_range_replay = events_df \
        .filter(
            (col("original_timestamp") >= time_range_start) &
            (col("original_timestamp") <= time_range_end)
        ) \
        .withColumn("replay_timestamp", current_timestamp()) \
        .withColumn("replay_window_start", lit(time_range_start).cast(TimestampType())) \
        .withColumn("replay_window_end", lit(time_range_end).cast(TimestampType())) \
        .withColumn("replay_reason", lit("time_range_analysis"))
    
    print(f"\nTime Range Replay ({time_range_start} to {time_range_end}):")
    time_range_replay.select(
        "event_id", "user_id", "event_type", "original_timestamp", 
        "replay_window_start", "replay_window_end"
    ).show(truncate=False)
    
    # Replay Pattern 4: Replay with controlled timing (preserve original intervals)
    window_spec = Window.orderBy("original_timestamp")
    
    timed_replay = events_df \
        .withColumn("event_sequence", row_number().over(window_spec)) \
        .withColumn("prev_timestamp", 
            lag("original_timestamp", 1).over(window_spec)
        ) \
        .withColumn("time_diff_seconds",
            when(col("prev_timestamp").isNotNull(),
                unix_timestamp(col("original_timestamp")) - 
                unix_timestamp(col("prev_timestamp"))
            ).otherwise(0)
        ) \
        .withColumn("cumulative_delay_seconds",
            _sum("time_diff_seconds").over(
                window_spec.rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow)
            )
        ) \
        .withColumn("replay_timestamp",
            expr("current_timestamp() + INTERVAL cumulative_delay_seconds SECONDS")
        )
    
    print("\nTimed Replay (preserving original time intervals):")
    timed_replay.select(
        "event_sequence", "event_id", "event_type", "time_diff_seconds", 
        "cumulative_delay_seconds", "original_timestamp", "replay_timestamp"
    ).show(truncate=False)
    
    # Replay Pattern 5: Replay with transformation/correction
    corrected_replay = events_df \
        .withColumn("replay_timestamp", current_timestamp()) \
        .withColumn("corrected_status",
            when(
                (col("event_type") == "purchase") & (col("status") == "failed"),
                "success"  # Simulate fixing the issue
            ).otherwise(col("status"))
        ) \
        .withColumn("was_corrected",
            col("status") != col("corrected_status")
        ) \
        .withColumn("replay_reason",
            when(col("was_corrected"), "data_correction")
            .otherwise("standard_replay")
        )
    
    print("\nReplay with Corrections:")
    corrected_replay.select(
        "event_id", "event_type", "status", "corrected_status", 
        "was_corrected", "replay_reason"
    ).show(truncate=False)
    
    # Replay Pattern 6: Replay audit trail
    replay_audit = full_replay \
        .select(
            col("event_id"),
            col("user_id"),
            col("event_type"),
            col("original_timestamp"),
            col("replay_timestamp"),
            col("replay_version"),
            col("replay_reason")
        ) \
        .withColumn("replay_duration_seconds",
            unix_timestamp(col("replay_timestamp")) - 
            unix_timestamp(col("original_timestamp"))
        ) \
        .withColumn("audit_id", monotonically_increasing_id()) \
        .withColumn("audit_timestamp", current_timestamp())
    
    print("\nReplay Audit Trail:")
    replay_audit.select(
        "audit_id", "event_id", "event_type", "replay_version", 
        "replay_reason", "replay_duration_seconds"
    ).show(truncate=False)
    
    # Replay Pattern 7: Comparison between original and replay results
    # Simulate processing results
    original_results = events_df \
        .groupBy("user_id") \
        .agg(
            count("*").alias("original_event_count"),
            count(when(col("status") == "success", 1)).alias("original_success_count"),
            count(when(col("status") == "failed", 1)).alias("original_failed_count")
        )
    
    replay_results = corrected_replay \
        .groupBy("user_id") \
        .agg(
            count("*").alias("replay_event_count"),
            count(when(col("corrected_status") == "success", 1)).alias("replay_success_count"),
            count(when(col("corrected_status") == "failed", 1)).alias("replay_failed_count")
        )
    
    comparison = original_results.join(replay_results, "user_id", "outer") \
        .withColumn("success_diff", 
            col("replay_success_count") - col("original_success_count")
        ) \
        .withColumn("failed_diff",
            col("replay_failed_count") - col("original_failed_count")
        )
    
    print("\nOriginal vs Replay Results Comparison:")
    comparison.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Replay Pattern 8: Incremental replay (replay only new events since last replay)
    last_replay_timestamp = "2024-01-15 10:15:00"
    
    incremental_replay = events_df \
        .filter(col("original_timestamp") > last_replay_timestamp) \
        .withColumn("replay_timestamp", current_timestamp()) \
        .withColumn("last_replay_timestamp", lit(last_replay_timestamp).cast(TimestampType())) \
        .withColumn("replay_type", lit("incremental")) \
        .withColumn("is_new_event", lit(True))
    
    print(f"\nIncremental Replay (events after {last_replay_timestamp}):")
    incremental_replay.select(
        "event_id", "event_type", "original_timestamp", 
        "last_replay_timestamp", "replay_type", "is_new_event"
    ).show(truncate=False)
    
    return events_df

def streaming_event_processing_example():
    """
    Bonus: Example of applying these patterns to streaming data

    For Streaming Event Processing with Structured Streaming:
    
    # Create streaming DataFrame
    streaming_df = spark.readStream \\
        .format("kafka") \\
        .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", "localhost:9092") \\
        .option("subscribe", "events") \\
        .load()
    
    # Apply Event Filtering Pattern
    filtered_stream = streaming_df.filter(col("value") > 100)
    
    # Apply Event Aggregation Pattern with Watermarking
    aggregated_stream = streaming_df \\
        .withWatermark("timestamp", "10 minutes") \\
        .groupBy(
            window(col("timestamp"), "5 minutes"),
            col("event_type")
        ) \\
        .agg(count("*").alias("count"))
    
    # Apply Out-of-Order Event Pattern
    query = aggregated_stream.writeStream \\
        .outputMode("update") \\
        .format("console") \\
        .option("truncate", "false") \\
        .start()
    
    # Watermarking handles late data automatically
    # Events arriving within watermark window are processed
    # Events outside watermark are dropped
    """)

def round_robin_distribution():
    """
    Round-robin distributes data evenly across partitions.
    Each record is assigned to partitions sequentially.
    """
    # Create sample dataset
    data = [(i, f"user_{i}", i * 100) for i in range(1, 21)]
    df = spark.createDataFrame(data, ["id", "username", "amount"])
    
    print("\nOriginal Data:")
    df.show()
    
    # Method 1: Using repartition() - creates even distribution
    num_partitions = 4
    df_round_robin = df.repartition(num_partitions)
    
    print(f"\nRound-Robin Distribution across {num_partitions} partitions:")
    print(f"Number of partitions: {df_round_robin.rdd.getNumPartitions()}")
    
    # Show distribution of records across partitions
    def count_partition(iterator):
        yield sum(1 for _ in iterator)
    
    partition_counts = df_round_robin.rdd.mapPartitions(count_partition).collect()
    for i, count in enumerate(partition_counts):
        print(f"Partition {i}: {count} records")
    
    # Method 2: Custom round-robin using monotonically_increasing_id
    df_with_index = df.withColumn("row_id", monotonically_increasing_id())
    df_custom_rr = df_with_index.withColumn(
        "partition_id", 
        col("row_id") % num_partitions
    ).repartition(num_partitions, "partition_id")
    
    print("\nCustom Round-Robin with explicit partition assignment:")
    df_custom_rr.select("id", "username", "partition_id").show()
    
    return df_round_robin

def hash_distribution():
    """
    Hash distribution ensures records with same key go to same partition.
    Critical for join optimization and aggregation operations.
    """
    # Create sample dataset with customer orders
    orders_data = [
        (1, "CUST001", "2024-01-01", 100),
        (2, "CUST002", "2024-01-01", 200),
        (3, "CUST001", "2024-01-02", 150),
        (4, "CUST003", "2024-01-02", 300),
        (5, "CUST002", "2024-01-03", 250),
        (6, "CUST001", "2024-01-03", 175),
        (7, "CUST004", "2024-01-04", 400),
        (8, "CUST003", "2024-01-04", 350),
        (9, "CUST002", "2024-01-05", 225),
        (10, "CUST004", "2024-01-05", 450)
    ]
    
    df_orders = spark.createDataFrame(
        orders_data, 
        ["order_id", "customer_id", "order_date", "amount"]
    )
    
    print("\nOriginal Orders Data:")
    df_orders.show()
    
    # Hash distribution by customer_id
    num_partitions = 4
    df_hash = df_orders.repartition(num_partitions, "customer_id")
    
    print(f"\nHash Distribution by customer_id across {num_partitions} partitions:")
    print(f"Number of partitions: {df_hash.rdd.getNumPartitions()}")
    
    # Show which partition each customer's data lands in
    df_with_partition = df_hash.withColumn(
        "partition_id", 
        spark_partition_id()
    )
    
    print("\nData distribution by partition:")
    df_with_partition.groupBy("partition_id", "customer_id") \
        .agg(count("*").alias("record_count")) \
        .orderBy("partition_id", "customer_id") \
        .show()
    
    # Custom hash function example
    def custom_hash_partition(key, num_partitions):
        """Custom hash function using Python's hashlib"""
        hash_value = int(hashlib.md5(str(key).encode()).hexdigest(), 16)
        return hash_value % num_partitions
    
    # Register UDF for custom hashing
    hash_udf = udf(lambda x: custom_hash_partition(x, num_partitions), IntegerType())
    
    df_custom_hash = df_orders.withColumn(
        "custom_partition", 
        hash_udf(col("customer_id"))
    )
    
    print("\nCustom Hash Distribution:")
    df_custom_hash.select("order_id", "customer_id", "custom_partition").show()
    
    return df_hash

def range_distribution():
    """
    Range distribution partitions data based on value ranges.
    Useful for maintaining sort order and range queries.
    """
    # Create sample dataset with timestamps
    from datetime import datetime, timedelta
    
    base_date = datetime(2024, 1, 1)
    sales_data = [
        (i, 
         f"PROD{i%5}", 
         (base_date + timedelta(days=i)).strftime("%Y-%m-%d"),
         100 + (i * 10))
        for i in range(1, 31)
    ]
    
    df_sales = spark.createDataFrame(
        sales_data,
        ["sale_id", "product_id", "sale_date", "amount"]
    )
    
    print("\nOriginal Sales Data:")
    df_sales.show(10)
    
    # Range partitioning by amount
    num_partitions = 4
    df_range = df_sales.repartitionByRange(num_partitions, "amount")
    
    print(f"\nRange Distribution by amount across {num_partitions} partitions:")
    
    df_with_partition = df_range.withColumn(
        "partition_id",
        spark_partition_id()
    )
    
    # Show range distribution statistics
    print("\nPartition Statistics:")
    df_with_partition.groupBy("partition_id") \
        .agg(
            min("amount").alias("min_amount"),
            max("amount").alias("max_amount"),
            count("*").alias("record_count")
        ) \
        .orderBy("partition_id") \
        .show()
    
    # Custom range partitioning example
    def assign_range_partition(amount):
        """Custom range assignment based on business logic"""
        if amount < 150:
            return 0  # Low value
        elif amount < 250:
            return 1  # Medium value
        elif amount < 350:
            return 2  # High value
        else:
            return 3  # Very high value
    
    range_udf = udf(assign_range_partition, IntegerType())
    
    df_custom_range = df_sales.withColumn(
        "custom_range_partition",
        range_udf(col("amount"))
    )
    
    print("\nCustom Range Distribution:")
    df_custom_range.groupBy("custom_range_partition") \
        .agg(
            min("amount").alias("min_amount"),
            max("amount").alias("max_amount"),
            count("*").alias("count")
        ) \
        .orderBy("custom_range_partition") \
        .show()
    
    # Time-based range partitioning
    df_time_range = df_sales.repartitionByRange(num_partitions, "sale_date")
    
    print("\nTime-based Range Distribution:")
    df_time_partition = df_time_range.withColumn(
        "partition_id",
        spark_partition_id()
    )
    
    df_time_partition.groupBy("partition_id") \
        .agg(
            min("sale_date").alias("min_date"),
            max("sale_date").alias("max_date"),
            count("*").alias("count")
        ) \
        .orderBy("partition_id") \
        .show()
    
    return df_range

def replicated_distribution():
    """
    Replicated distribution copies entire dataset to all executors.
    Used for small reference data that needs to be available everywhere.
    """
    # Create small dimension table (countries)
    countries_data = [
        ("US", "United States", "North America"),
        ("UK", "United Kingdom", "Europe"),
        ("JP", "Japan", "Asia"),
        ("DE", "Germany", "Europe"),
        ("CA", "Canada", "North America")
    ]
    
    df_countries = spark.createDataFrame(
        countries_data,
        ["country_code", "country_name", "region"]
    )
    
    # Create larger fact table (transactions)
    import random
    transactions_data = [
        (i, 
         random.choice(["US", "UK", "JP", "DE", "CA"]),
         f"PROD{i%10}",
         random.randint(100, 1000))
        for i in range(1, 101)
    ]
    
    df_transactions = spark.createDataFrame(
        transactions_data,
        ["transaction_id", "country_code", "product_id", "amount"]
    )
    
    print("\nDimension Table (Countries) - Small, will be replicated:")
    df_countries.show()
    
    print("\nFact Table (Transactions) - Large, sample:")
    df_transactions.show(10)
    
    # Method 1: Using broadcast for replication
    from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast
    
    print("\nReplication using Broadcast Join:")
    df_result = df_transactions.join(
        broadcast(df_countries),  # Replicate countries to all nodes
        "country_code"
    )
    
    print("Join Result (first 10 rows):")
    df_result.select(
        "transaction_id", "country_code", "country_name", 
        "region", "amount"
    ).show(10)
    
    # Show execution plan to verify broadcast
    print("\nExecution Plan (notice BroadcastHashJoin):")
    df_result.explain()
    
    # Method 2: Explicit replication using cache
    print("\nMethod 2: Explicit Replication using Cache:")
    
    # Replicate by caching on all executors
    df_countries_cached = df_countries.cache()
    df_countries_cached.count()  # Trigger caching
    
    print(f"Countries table cached: {df_countries_cached.is_cached}")
    print(f"Storage Level: {df_countries_cached.storageLevel}")
    
    # Verify data is available on all partitions
    num_partitions = 4
    df_transactions_partitioned = df_transactions.repartition(num_partitions)
    
    # Join with cached (replicated) dimension table
    df_joined = df_transactions_partitioned.join(
        df_countries_cached,
        "country_code"
    )
    
    print("\nTransactions by Region:")
    df_joined.groupBy("region") \
        .agg(
            count("*").alias("transaction_count"),
            sum("amount").alias("total_amount")
        ) \
        .show()
    
    return df_result

        "category", "quantity", "price"
    ).show(10)
    
    # Calculate revenue
    df_revenue = df_broadcast_join.withColumn(
        "revenue",
        col("quantity") * col("price")
    )
    
    print("\nRevenue Analysis by Category:")
    df_revenue.groupBy("category") \
        .agg(
            count("*").alias("sales_count"),
            sum("quantity").alias("total_quantity"),
            sum("revenue").alias("total_revenue")
        ) \
        .orderBy(desc("total_revenue")) \
        .show()
    
    # Compare with regular join (without broadcast)
    print("\n--- REGULAR JOIN (Without Broadcast) ---")
    df_regular_join = df_sales.join(
        df_products,
        "product_id",
        "inner"
    )
    
    print("\nRegular Join Execution Plan:")
    df_regular_join.explain()
    
    print("\n--- BROADCAST JOIN Execution Plan ---")
    df_broadcast_join.explain()
    
    # Broadcast with multiple conditions
    print("\n--- Advanced Broadcast Pattern ---")
    
    # Create another small dimension table (stores)
    stores_data = [
        ("STORE01", "New York", "East"),
        ("STORE02", "Los Angeles", "West"),
        ("STORE03", "Chicago", "Central"),
        ("STORE04", "Houston", "South"),
        ("STORE05", "Phoenix", "West")
    ]
    
    df_stores = spark.createDataFrame(
        stores_data,
        ["store_id", "city", "region"]
    )
    
    # Add store_id to sales
    df_sales_with_store = df_sales.withColumn(
        "store_id",
        concat(lit("STORE"), 
               lpad((col("sale_id") % 5 + 1).cast("string"), 2, "0"))
    )
    
    # Multiple broadcast joins
    df_complete = df_sales_with_store \
        .join(broadcast(df_products), "product_id") \
        .join(broadcast(df_stores), "store_id")
    
    print("\nMultiple Broadcast Joins Result:")
    df_complete.select(
        "sale_id", "product_name", "city", "region", "quantity"
    ).show(10)
    
    print("\nSales by Region and Category:")
    df_complete.groupBy("region", "category") \
        .agg(
            count("*").alias("sales_count"),
            sum(col("quantity") * col("price")).alias("revenue")
        ) \
        .orderBy("region", desc("revenue")) \
        .show()
    
    # Broadcast threshold configuration
    print("\n--- Broadcast Configuration ---")
    print(f"Auto Broadcast Join Threshold: {spark.conf.get('spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold')}")
    
    # Manual broadcast hint
    df_products.createOrReplaceTempView("products")
    df_sales.createOrReplaceTempView("sales")
    
    sql_broadcast = spark.sql("""
        SELECT /*+ BROADCAST(p) */
            s.sale_id,
            p.product_name,
            p.category,
            s.quantity,
            p.price,
            s.quantity * p.price as revenue
        FROM sales s
        INNER JOIN products p ON s.product_id = p.product_id
        LIMIT 10
    """)
    
    print("\nSQL Broadcast Join with Hint:")
    sql_broadcast.show()
    
    return df_broadcast_join

def compare_distribution_patterns():
    """
    Compare all distribution patterns with performance metrics
    """
    # Create test dataset
    test_data = [(i, f"key_{i%100}", i * 10, f"value_{i}") 
                 for i in range(1, 10001)]
    df_test = spark.createDataFrame(
        test_data,
        ["id", "key", "amount", "value"]
    )
    
    print("\nTest Dataset Summary:")
    print(f"Total Records: {df_test.count()}")
    print(f"Distinct Keys: {df_test.select('key').distinct().count()}")
    
    num_partitions = 8
    
    # 1. Round-Robin
    print("\n1. ROUND-ROBIN DISTRIBUTION:")
    df_rr = df_test.repartition(num_partitions)
    print(f"   Partitions: {df_rr.rdd.getNumPartitions()}")
    
    partition_sizes_rr = df_rr.rdd.mapPartitions(
        lambda it: [sum(1 for _ in it)]
    ).collect()
    print(f"   Records per partition: {partition_sizes_rr}")
    print(f"   Standard Deviation: {__import__('statistics').stdev(partition_sizes_rr):.2f}")
    
    # 2. Hash Distribution
    print("\n2. HASH DISTRIBUTION:")
    df_hash = df_test.repartition(num_partitions, "key")
    print(f"   Partitions: {df_hash.rdd.getNumPartitions()}")
    
    partition_sizes_hash = df_hash.rdd.mapPartitions(
        lambda it: [sum(1 for _ in it)]
    ).collect()
    print(f"   Records per partition: {partition_sizes_hash}")
    print(f"   Standard Deviation: {__import__('statistics').stdev(partition_sizes_hash):.2f}")
    
    # 3. Range Distribution
    print("\n3. RANGE DISTRIBUTION:")
    df_range = df_test.repartitionByRange(num_partitions, "amount")
    print(f"   Partitions: {df_range.rdd.getNumPartitions()}")
    
    partition_sizes_range = df_range.rdd.mapPartitions(
        lambda it: [sum(1 for _ in it)]
    ).collect()
    print(f"   Records per partition: {partition_sizes_range}")
    print(f"   Standard Deviation: {__import__('statistics').stdev(partition_sizes_range):.2f}")
    
    # Summary table
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("DISTRIBUTION PATTERN COMPARISON SUMMARY")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    summary_data = [
        ("Round-Robin", "Even", "No", "Load balancing", "General purpose"),
        ("Hash", "Even (same key)", "Yes", "Co-location", "Joins, GroupBy"),
        ("Range", "Varies", "Sorted", "Range queries", "Sorted operations"),
        ("Replicated", "Full copy", "Yes", "Lookup tables", "Small dimensions"),
        ("Broadcast", "Full copy", "Yes", "Join optimization", "Small tables in joins")
    ]
    
    df_summary = spark.createDataFrame(
        summary_data,
        ["Pattern", "Distribution", "Deterministic", "Best For", "Use Case"]
    )
    
    df_summary.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Performance characteristics
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("PERFORMANCE CHARACTERISTICS")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    perf_data = [
        ("Round-Robin", "O(1)", "Low", "Minimal", "High"),
        ("Hash", "O(1)", "Medium", "Medium", "Medium"),
        ("Range", "O(log n)", "Medium", "Medium", "Low"),
        ("Replicated", "O(n)", "High", "High", "Low"),
        ("Broadcast", "O(n)", "High", "High", "Very Low")
    ]
    
    df_perf = spark.createDataFrame(
        perf_data,
        ["Pattern", "Complexity", "Memory", "Network", "Shuffle"]
    )
    
    df_perf.show(truncate=False)

def practical_use_cases():
    """
    Real-world scenarios demonstrating when to use each pattern
    """
    
    # Use Case 1: E-commerce Order Processing
    print("\n--- Use Case 1: E-commerce Order Processing ---")
    
    # Orders (large table) - use hash distribution by customer_id
    orders = spark.createDataFrame([
        (i, f"CUST{i%500}", f"ORDER{i}", 100 + i)
        for i in range(1, 5001)
    ], ["order_id", "customer_id", "order_number", "amount"])
    
    # Customers (medium table) - use hash distribution
    customers = spark.createDataFrame([
        (f"CUST{i}", f"Customer {i}", f"email{i}@example.com")
        for i in range(500)
    ], ["customer_id", "name", "email"])
    
    # Product categories (small table) - use broadcast
    categories = spark.createDataFrame([
        ("CAT1", "Electronics", 0.1),
        ("CAT2", "Clothing", 0.15),
        ("CAT3", "Books", 0.05),
        ("CAT4", "Home", 0.12)
    ], ["category_id", "category_name", "tax_rate"])
    
    # Hash distribute orders and customers for efficient join
    orders_hash = orders.repartition(8, "customer_id")
    customers_hash = customers.repartition(8, "customer_id")
    
    # Broadcast small category table
    result = orders_hash.join(customers_hash, "customer_id") \
        .withColumn("category_id", lit("CAT1")) \
        .join(broadcast(categories), "category_id")
    
    print("E-commerce processing with mixed distribution:")
    result.select("order_number", "name", "category_name", "amount").show(5)
    
    # Use Case 2: Time-Series Data Analysis
    print("\n--- Use Case 2: Time-Series Data Analysis ---")
    
    from datetime import datetime, timedelta
    
    # Sensor data - use range distribution by timestamp
    base_time = datetime(2024, 1, 1)
    sensor_data = spark.createDataFrame([
        (i, f"SENSOR{i%10}", 
         (base_time + timedelta(hours=i)).strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"),
         20.0 + (i % 30))
        for i in range(1000)
    ], ["reading_id", "sensor_id", "timestamp", "temperature"])
    
    # Range partition by timestamp for time-based queries
    sensor_range = sensor_data.repartitionByRange(4, "timestamp")
    
    print("Time-series data with range distribution:")
    sensor_range.withColumn("partition", spark_partition_id()) \
        .groupBy("partition") \
        .agg(
            min("timestamp").alias("start_time"),
            max("timestamp").alias("end_time"),
            count("*").alias("readings")
        ) \
        .orderBy("partition") \
        .show()
    
    # Use Case 3: Machine Learning Feature Engineering
    print("\n--- Use Case 3: ML Feature Engineering ---")
    
    # Training data - round-robin for even distribution
    ml_data = spark.createDataFrame([
        (i, i * 0.5, i * 0.3, i % 2)
        for i in range(10000)
    ], ["id", "feature1", "feature2", "label"])
    
    # Round-robin distribution for balanced training
    ml_distributed = ml_data.repartition(8)
    
    print("ML data with round-robin distribution:")
    print(f"Total samples: {ml_distributed.count()}")
    
    partition_counts = ml_distributed.rdd.mapPartitions(
        lambda it: [sum(1 for _ in it)]
    ).collect()
    print(f"Samples per partition: {partition_counts}")
    print(f"Balance score (std dev): {__import__('statistics').stdev(partition_counts):.2f}")

        1. ROUND-ROBIN DISTRIBUTION:
           ✓ Use when: No natural partitioning key exists
           ✓ Benefits: Perfect load balancing
           ✗ Avoid: When data locality matters
           
        2. HASH DISTRIBUTION:
           ✓ Use when: Joining or grouping by specific keys
           ✓ Benefits: Co-locates related data, reduces shuffle
           ✗ Avoid: When key distribution is highly skewed
           
        3. RANGE DISTRIBUTION:
           ✓ Use when: Data needs to be sorted or range queries are common
           ✓ Benefits: Maintains sort order, efficient range scans
           ✗ Avoid: When data ranges are imbalanced
           
        4. REPLICATED DISTRIBUTION:
           ✓ Use when: Small reference data needed everywhere
           ✓ Benefits: No network transfer during access
           ✗ Avoid: For large datasets (memory constraints)
           
        5. BROADCAST DISTRIBUTION:
           ✓ Use when: Joining large table with small table (<10MB)
           ✓ Benefits: Eliminates shuffle, significant performance gain
           ✗ Avoid: When broadcast table is too large
           
        CONFIGURATION TIPS:
        - Set spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold appropriately (default: 10MB)
        - Use spark.sql.shuffle.partitions based on data size (default: 200)
        - Monitor partition skew using spark.sql.adaptive.enabled
        - Consider spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled for skewed data
        """
        
        print(best_practices)
        
        print("\n" + "=" * 80)
        print("ALL DEMONSTRATIONS COMPLETED SUCCESSFULLY")
        print("=" * 80)
        
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"\nError occurred: {str(e)}")
        import traceback
        traceback.print_exc()
    
    finally:
        # Clean up
        print("\nCleaning up resources...")
        spark.catalog.clearCache()
        # spark.stop()  # Uncomment if you want to stop the session
